newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Risky for Finland outside ERM - central bank.
newsitem.headline: Risky for Finland outside ERM - central bank.

text.p: Bank of Finland governor Sirkka Hamalainen said on Tuesday that Finland, eager to be among the first to join monetary union, was taking a risk by being outside Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM).

She said there would be a need for flexibility in the interpretation of the Maastricht treaty's exchange rate criterion for Finland to be able to join planned economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start in 1999.
"It is needed if we want to be among the first (in EMU)," Hamalainen said.
Hamalainen, speaking at the European Parliament in Brussels, refused to comment on whether the country would link the markka to the ERM, which groups 10 of the bloc's 15 currencies.
But she said Finland had already taken a risk when it did not join this spring.

She was referring to the Maastricht treaty single currency criterion which suggests a country should be in ERM two years before EU leaders in early 1998 decide which countries qualify for the single currency.
"We have already taken the risk," Hamalainen said.
But she added that she believed there may be some flexibility on the issue. "The question is how long membership is needed," she said.
Some countries, especially Sweden and Britain, argue that it is currency stability, not ERM membership in itself, that should be the key for meeting the Maastricht treaty currency requirement.
The issue will not be finally settled until EU leaders take their decision in 1998.

The Finnish government has said that Finland will have to decide this autumn on whether to link the markka to the ERM, which limits fluctuations between participating currencies to 15 percent up or down.
Many economists expect a link to come after Finland's local and European elections on October 20.
Hamalainen said that the Maastricht treaty was clear; membership of the ERM and currency stability for two years is one of the conditions for joining the single currency.
She said the Finnish markka had been stable for two years and that the Bank expected it to remain so.
Hamalainen added that membership of the ERM in itself was not enough, referring to the current wide fluctuation bands.
When the Maastricht treaty was agreed by EU leaders in December 1991 the bands were 2.25 percent for most currencies.
Apart from the requirement on currency stability, a country must meet criteria on debt, borrowing, interest rates and inflation to qualify for the single currency.

Finland already meets the inflation and interest rate criteria. Its budget deficit is forecast at 1.4 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, well below the three percent-limit in the Maastricht treaty, while the debt level is expected to be near the maximum allowed level of 60 percent of GDP.
